articles.title: All things pass

statement.t: All things change, and I with them; the change is the work of nature and nothing bad, and nothing that passes is great.

parts.words: All things change, and I with them
the change is the work of nature

statement.kind: A fact, its source and two judgments
statement.form: Claim 1 states the fact: all things change, quickly, and I with them. Claim 2 gives its source, the nature of the whole, which loves change and keeps to one kind. The statement then sets two judgments side by side: change is nothing bad (claim 5) and nothing that passes is great (claim 3). Claim 4 is the exercise that keeps the fact in view, and claim 6 says what holds without nature.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five claims gain a second author: that all things change and I with them, that I look down on what passes, the practice of seeing all of time, that a loss is only a change, and that what ceases to be does not perish but is dissolved. The ground gains one good that does not die; what breaks gains the fear of a death already under way and the weariness that sameness can breed. He backs the third claim’s contempt for what passes in Letter 58 and limits it in Letter 98: what I lose I keep in memory, with thanks.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, and he adds what Marcus’s section does not name: a good that does not pass, the true good of wisdom and virtue.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I myself, while I say that these things are changing, have changed.
piece.follows: Seneca himself changes even while he speaks about change.
piece.context: Letter 58, on Plato’s classes of being: what we see and touch is in flux, our bodies above all. By “these things” Seneca means what we see and touch.
gives: I am changing with them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: The world too, an eternal and unconquerable thing, changes and does not remain the same.
piece.follows: Even the world, which lasts for ever, changes and does not stay the same.
piece.context: Letter 58, after saying that a man flows away like a river: the world too keeps everything it had, but always in a new arrangement.
gives: All things are changing

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us despise all the things that are so far from precious that it is doubtful whether they exist at all.
piece.follows: We should look down on things of so little worth that we can doubt they exist at all.
piece.context: Letter 58 draws a use from Plato: what the senses show is in flux and not truly real. The things “so far from precious” are those passing things.
gives: I look down on everything mortal

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Set before yourself the vastness of deep time and take in the whole; then compare this thing we call a human lifetime with the immeasurable.
piece.follows: I should picture all of time and take in the whole, and set a human lifetime against the immeasurable.
piece.context: Letter 99 consoles a father whose young son has died. Set against the whole of time, Seneca says, a long life is little more than a child’s.
gives: the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: all the things that seem to perish are changed
piece.follows: What seems to perish only changes.
piece.context: Letter 36 answers a craving for longer life: nothing that vanishes from sight is annihilated. The “things that seem to perish” include our own death.
gives: a loss is nothing but a change

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.
piece.follows: Everything that exists will cease to be, yet it does not perish but is dissolved.
piece.context: Letter 71: everything, the stars and the earth included, is born, grows and is extinguished. Here “whatever is” means each of those things.
gives: a thing’s death is only its dissolution

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: they are surprised to lose anything themselves, though on one day they are going to lose everything
piece.follows: It makes no sense to be surprised at losing one thing when one is going to lose everything.
piece.context: Letter 98, on the fickleness of Fortune: people forget where each day pushes them. To “lose anything” is to lose their goods, and in the end their life.
gives: it is ridiculous to be surprised or annoyed at it

items.label: why
items.role: One good that does not pass
items.t: All the good things that mortals chase are mortal too. The true good, which is wisdom and virtue, does not die: it is the only lasting thing a mortal can have.
items.why: Marcus says here that nothing that passes is great, and 12.25 names one great thing, acting as my nature leads. He does not say that anything does not pass. Seneca names it: the true good, wisdom and virtue, does not die.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: “Every good of mortals is mortal.”
support.follows: Every good that mortals have is itself mortal.
support.context: Letter 98 quotes Metrodorus, consoling his sister for the death of her son. The “good of mortals” is the goods people rush to in crowds.
gives: All the good things that mortals chase are mortal too

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For that true good does not die; it is sure and everlasting: wisdom and virtue. This is the one immortal thing that falls to mortals.
support.follows: The true good, wisdom and virtue, does not die; it is the one immortal thing a mortal can have.
support.context: Letter 98, Seneca’s comment on Metrodorus’s saying that every good of mortals is mortal: the true good is the one exception.
gives: The true good, which is wisdom and virtue, does not die
it is the only lasting thing a mortal can have

items.label: breaks
items.role: A death that happens every day
items.t: When I fear that death will come to me once, I forget that it comes every day: every moment is the death of what I was, and the last hour only completes it.
items.why: Marcus says that I am in continual alteration and in a certain respect perishing (9.17), but he draws nothing from it about the fear of death. Seneca does: what I fear as one future event is already happening.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: every moment is the death of the state before it. Come, do not fear that what happens every day may happen once!
support.follows: Each moment ends what we were before, so it is foolish to fear that death will happen once.
support.context: Letter 58: after Heraclitus’s river, Seneca says that we too are carried past as fast. By “what happens every day” he means death.
gives: When I fear that death will come to me once
it comes every day
every moment is the death of what I was

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the last hour, in which we cease to be, does not alone make death but alone completes it.
support.follows: The last hour of life does not make death by itself; it only completes a dying that was already under way.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: we die every day, as a water clock empties drop by drop. The “last hour” is the moment we cease to be.
gives: the last hour only completes it

items.label: breaks
items.t: Seeing that I do nothing new and see nothing new can make me sick of living. The wish to die that grows from that weariness is a passion, and I avoid it.
items.why: Marcus draws comfort from sameness: nothing new comes that I need fear (8.5), and forty years show as much as ten thousand (7.27). Seneca shows the same thought turning into weariness of life, a failure Marcus does not name here.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Some people are overcome by having had their fill of doing and seeing the same things, and by not hatred of life but distaste for it.
support.follows: Some people want to die not because they hate life but because they are sick of doing and seeing the same things.
support.context: Letter 24, on the urge to die: besides those who scorn life and those who find it a burden, some are overcome by weariness. The “distaste for it” is a distaste for life.
gives: can make me sick of living

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do nothing new, I see nothing new: at some point there comes nausea at this too.
support.follows: Whoever thinks that he does and sees nothing new will at some point grow sick of it.
support.context: Letter 24: the words Seneca gives to a man who has had his fill of life, who sees nature go round and return. By “this” he means that endless round.
gives: Seeing that I do nothing new and see nothing new

support.author: seneca
support.quote: above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying.
support.follows: The brave and wise man should above all avoid the lust for dying.
support.context: Letter 24: the brave and wise man should not flee from life. By “that passion” Seneca means the lust for dying, which seizes the noble and the spiritless alike.
gives: The wish to die that grows from that weariness is a passion, and I avoid it

items.t: In Letter 58 Seneca, like Marcus, tells me to despise what passes (Ep. 58.28); in Letter 98 he tells me to keep what I have lost in memory and to be thankful for having had it. Chance can take the thing from me, but not the fact that I had it. This limits claim 3 and does not contradict it: Marcus’s word in 9.27, “look down on”, can also mean simply to think little of.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: that we hold in memory the things lost, and do not let the fruit we gathered from them drop away along with the things themselves
support.follows: We should hold in memory what we have lost, and not let the fruit we gathered from it drop away with it.
support.context: Letter 98 asks what help we have against losses. The “things lost” are goods, and the people we loved.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Having is snatched away; having had, never.
support.follows: What we have can be taken from us; that we had it cannot.
support.context: Letter 98, on losses brought by Fortune: having a thing can be taken away, having had it cannot.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is a thoroughly ungrateful man who, when he has lost a thing, owes nothing for having received it.
support.follows: It is deeply ungrateful to lose something and think nothing is owed for having had it.
support.context: Letter 98, on losses brought by Fortune: whoever loses a thing still owes thanks for having received it.

passages.title: On being, Plato's ideas and old age
passages.text: The fifth kind is of the things that exist in the common way; these begin to concern us; here are all things: people, cattle, objects. The sixth kind is of the things that, so to speak, exist, such as the void, such as time. Whatever we see or touch, Plato does not count among the things that he thinks exist in the proper sense; for they flow, and are in constant loss and gain. None of us is the same in old age as he was when young; none of us is the same in the morning as he was the day before. Our bodies are swept along in the manner of rivers. Whatever you see runs with time; nothing of the things we see remains; I myself, while I say that these things are changing, have changed.

passages.title: On being, Plato's ideas and old age
passages.text: I have spoken of man, matter that is flowing and perishable and at the mercy of every cause. The world too, an eternal and unconquerable thing, changes and does not remain the same. For although it has in itself all that it had, it has it otherwise than it had it: it changes its order.

passages.title: On being, Plato's ideas and old age
passages.text: For all things remain, not because they are eternal, but because they are defended by the care of the one who governs them: immortal things would need no guardian. These things the craftsman preserves, overcoming the frailty of matter by his own power. Let us despise all the things that are so far from precious that it is doubtful whether they exist at all.

passages.title: On excessive grief for a lost child
passages.text: “But he died a boy.” I am not yet saying that the one who is done with life is better off. Let us pass to the one who has grown old: by how little he beats the infant! Set before yourself the vastness of deep time and take in the whole; then compare this thing we call a human lifetime with the immeasurable. You will see how small a thing it is that we wish for, that we stretch out.

passages.title: On the benefits of a quiet life
passages.text: But later I will show more carefully that all the things that seem to perish are changed. A man who is going to come back ought to go out with an even mind. Watch the circle of things as they return upon themselves: you will see that nothing in this world is extinguished, but that things go down and rise by turns. Summer has gone, but another year will bring it; winter has fallen away, its own months will bring it back; night has buried the sun, but day will at once drive night itself away. That running about of the stars comes back to whatever it has passed; one part of the sky is continually being lifted, one part is being sunk.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: All things move through fixed periods: they must be born, grow, be extinguished. Whatever you see running above us, and these things on which we lean and have been set as though they were the most solid of things, will be worn away and will cease. There is nothing that does not have its own old age. Nature sends these things off to the same place after unequal spans: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.

passages.title: On not depending on fortune's gifts
passages.text: But they are so shameless, and so forgetful of where they are going, of where each single day is pushing them, that they are surprised to lose anything themselves, though on one day they are going to lose everything. Whatever it is that you are written down as owner of is in your keeping; it is not yours. Nothing is firm for one who is not firm, nothing eternal and unconquerable for one who is fragile. It is as necessary to perish as to lose, and this very fact, if we understand it, is a comfort. Lose with an even mind: one must perish.

passages.title: On not depending on fortune's gifts
passages.text: So I think Metrodorus put it excellently in the letter in which he consoles his sister after the loss of her son, who was of the finest promise: “Every good of mortals is mortal.” He is speaking of these goods that people rush to in crowds. For that true good does not die; it is sure and everlasting: wisdom and virtue. This is the one immortal thing that falls to mortals.

passages.title: On being, Plato's ideas and old age
passages.text: This is what Heraclitus says: “Into the same river we go down twice and do not go down.” For the name of the river remains the same; the water has passed on. This is plainer in a river than in a human being; but a course no less swift carries us past too, and so I wonder at our madness, that we love so much a thing so quick to flee, the body, and fear that some day we may die, when every moment is the death of the state before it. Come, do not fear that what happens every day may happen once!

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: We die every day; for every day some part of life is taken away, and even at the time when we are growing, life is growing less. We have lost infancy, then childhood, then youth. Right up to yesterday, whatever time has passed has perished; this very day that we are living we share with death. Just as it is not the last drop that empties a water clock but whatever has run out before, so the last hour, in which we cease to be, does not alone make death but alone completes it. That is when we come to it, but we have been coming for a long time.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: Some people are overcome by having had their fill of doing and seeing the same things, and by not hatred of life but distaste for it. We slide into this with philosophy itself pushing us, while we say: “How long the same things? Of course I will wake, I will sleep, I will be hungry, I will be cold, I will be hot. Nothing has an end, but all things are linked in a circle; they flee and they follow. Night presses on day, day on night; summer ends in autumn, winter bears down on autumn, and is checked by spring. All things pass in such a way that they come back. I do nothing new, I see nothing new: at some point there comes nausea at this too.” There are many who judge living to be not bitter but superfluous. Farewell.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: A brave and wise man ought not to flee from life but to go out of it. And above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying. For there is, my Lucilius, as towards other things, so also towards dying, an unconsidered leaning of the mind, which often seizes men who are noble and of the keenest character, and often the spiritless and the downcast. The former scorn life; the latter find it a burden.

passages.title: On not depending on fortune's gifts
passages.text: What help, then, do we find against these losses? This: that we hold in memory the things lost, and do not let the fruit we gathered from them drop away along with the things themselves. Having is snatched away; having had, never. It is a thoroughly ungrateful man who, when he has lost a thing, owes nothing for having received it. Chance snatches the thing from us; the use and the fruit of it chance leaves with us, and this we ourselves have lost by the unfairness of our longing.

claims.t: All things are changing, and I am changing with them, all the time and quickly. The whole is like a river in flood: each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen.
claims.shared: 9.17 and 9.27 both say that all things change (“All things are in change”; earth “will change, and those things too will change without end”), and 9.17 and 6.14 both put the person among them. 4.35 and 9.27 both picture the whole as a rushing stream (“a violent current”; “a torrent”), and 4.35 and 6.14 both say that a thing is gone as soon as it is seen.
claims.changed: 9.17 speaks of the universe, 4.35 of eternity as a river, 9.27 of the substance of the whole as a torrent; the claim calls all three “the whole”. 2.9 speaks of things vanishing, not changing; the claim takes from it only the speed.

support.quote: All things are in change.
support.follows: Everything is changing.
gives: All things are changing

support.quote: You yourself too are in continual alteration and, in a certain respect, in perishing, and so is the whole universe.
support.follows: I too am always being altered, and in a way perishing, and so is the whole universe.
gives: I am changing with them
all the time

support.quote: Then earth itself will change, and those things too will change without end, and those again without end.
support.follows: Even the earth will change, and what it changes into will change again, without end.
gives: All things are changing

support.quote: Flows and alterations renew the universe continually
support.follows: The universe is renewed all the time by flows and alterations.
gives: All things are changing
all the time

support.quote: Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind: like the vapour that rises from blood and the breath drawn in from the air.
support.follows: A person’s life is a passing thing too, like vapour rising from blood or a breath drawn in.
gives: I am changing with them

support.quote: How quickly all things vanish, the bodies themselves into the universe, the memories of them into eternity.
support.follows: All things vanish quickly: bodies into the universe, and the memory of them into eternity.
gives: and quickly

support.quote: Eternity is a kind of river of things that come to be, and a violent current. For as soon as each thing has been seen it has been carried past, and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along.
support.follows: Time is like a fast river: each thing is swept past as soon as it is seen, and others follow it.
gives: and quickly
The whole is like a river in flood
each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen

support.quote: The substance of the whole is a torrent: it carries everything along.
support.follows: The stuff of which everything is made is like a torrent that sweeps all things along.
gives: The whole is like a river in flood

support.quote: It is as if someone began to love one of the little sparrows flying past, and it has already gone out of sight.
support.follows: Loving one of these passing things is like loving a sparrow that is out of sight the moment one notices it.
gives: each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen

claims.role: Nature’s work, always of one kind
claims.t: Changing things is the work of the nature of the whole, and it loves this work: it changes what exists and makes new things like the old. Nothing comes that is new in kind; what will be is of the same kind as what has been.
claims.shared: 4.29 and 9.33 both say that the nature of the whole loves change (“loves nothing so much as to change”; “in this the nature of the whole delights”) and that it makes new things like the old (“new things like them”; “others like them”). 6.34, 7.27 and 9.33 all say that what comes is “of the same kind” as what was.
claims.changed: 8.5 says that change is nature’s work and 4.29 that nature loves it; the claim puts the two in one sentence. “New in kind” is the editor’s wording for 8.5’s “nothing new” read beside 6.34’s “of the same kind”.

support.quote: The nature of the whole has this as its work: to move what is here over to there, to change it, to lift it from here and carry it there.
support.follows: The work of the nature of the whole is to move things from one place to another and to change them.
gives: Changing things is the work of the nature of the whole

support.quote: the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and make new things like them
support.follows: Nothing pleases the nature of the whole more than changing what exists and making new things like it.
gives: Changing things is the work of the nature of the whole
it loves this work
it changes what exists
makes new things like the old

support.quote: And in this the nature of the whole delights, the nature in accordance with which all things come about well, and from eternity have come about in the same kind of way, and without end there will be others like them.
support.follows: The nature of the whole delights in change, and things of the same kind as before will keep coming about without end.
gives: it loves this work
makes new things like the old
what will be is of the same kind as what has been

support.quote: All things are transformations, not so that one need fear something new. All things are familiar
support.follows: All things are changes of what was, so nothing new and strange comes that one need fear.
gives: Nothing comes that is new in kind

support.quote: Whoever has seen what is now has seen everything: all that has come to be from the everlasting past and all that will be without end. For all things are of the same stock and of the same kind.
support.follows: Whoever has seen the present has seen all past and future, since all things are of the same kind.
gives: Nothing comes that is new in kind
what will be is of the same kind as what has been

support.quote: It is possible to foresee what will be as well. For it will certainly be of the same kind, and it cannot step out of the rhythm of what is happening now.
support.follows: The future can be foreseen, because it will be of the same kind as what happens now.

claims.t: When I reflect on how fast things change and on how small a part of eternity and of substance is mine, I picture nothing that passes as great. I do not prize what runs past me, and I look down on everything mortal.
claims.shared: 9.27 and 12.25 both say that reflecting leads to holding things cheap (“a person who reflects on … will look down on everything mortal”; “Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great”). 6.14 and 2.9 say the same of what passes: no one would prize it, and it is “cheap and contemptible”.
claims.changed: 12.25 says “nothing” and names one exception, kept as a said-once item; the claim says “nothing that passes”. 9.27 says what a person who reflects will do; the claim says it of me.

support.quote: For a person who reflects on wave after wave of changes and alterations, and on their speed, will look down on everything mortal.
support.follows: Whoever thinks about how fast changes follow one another will look down on everything mortal.
gives: When I reflect
how fast things change
I look down on everything mortal

support.quote: How small a part of boundless, gaping eternity has been portioned out to each one: for it vanishes very quickly into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the whole of soul.
support.follows: Each of us has been given a tiny share of endless time, of all substance and of all soul.
gives: how small a part of eternity and of substance is mine

support.quote: Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great
support.follows: Whoever reflects on how small their share is should picture nothing as great.
gives: When I reflect
I picture nothing that passes as great

support.quote: In this river, then, which of these things running past would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on?
support.follows: Nothing running past in this river is worth prizing, since no one can stand on it.
gives: I do not prize what runs past me

support.quote: What all the things perceived by the senses are like, and above all those that lure with pleasure or frighten with pain or are loudly celebrated through vanity: how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead.
support.follows: The things of the senses, above all what tempts, frightens or is famous, are cheap, quick to perish and dead.
gives: I picture nothing that passes as great

claims.t: I constantly keep in mind the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists, and against all that exists each thing is a fig seed, and against all of time a turn of a drill. I fix my attention on each thing and think of it as changing, and already dissolving.
claims.shared: 10.19 and 9.31 both tell me to hold the whole of time and of what exists in mind (“the whole of eternity and the whole of substance”; “encompassed the whole universe in thought … surveying everlasting eternity”) and to think of each thing as it changes (“think of it as already dissolving and in change”; “thinking of the swift change of each particular thing”). 4.29 says to observe change “continually”, as 10.19 says “constantly”.
claims.changed: 10.19 and 4.29 are instructions to “you”, and 9.31 is a fragment without a main verb; the claim states them as what I do.

support.quote: An impression, constantly, of the whole of eternity and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, set against substance, a fig seed, and set against time, a turn of a drill.
support.follows: I should keep all of time and all substance always in view, and see each thing against them as a fig seed or a moment.
gives: I constantly keep in mind
the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists
against all that exists each thing is a fig seed, and against all of time a turn of a drill

support.quote: Fixing attention on each object, think of it as already dissolving and in change

gives: I fix my attention on each thing
think of it as changing
already dissolving

support.quote: By having encompassed the whole universe in thought, and by surveying everlasting eternity, and by thinking of the swift change of each particular thing
support.follows: One holds the whole universe and all of time in thought, and thinks of how fast each thing changes.
gives: the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists
think of it as changing

support.follows: I should keep observing that everything comes about through change.
gives: I constantly keep in mind

claims.t: When I say that everything goes badly, I forget that a loss is nothing but a change, and that change is nothing bad for what is changed. The elements I am made of change too, and do not grumble.
claims.shared: 9.33 and 10.7 both say that losing or perishing is only change (“Loss is nothing other than change”; “let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered””). 4.35 and 10.7 both deny that change is bad for what is changed.
claims.changed: 9.33 asks “you” why you say that all goes badly; the claim makes it my failure. 8.16 adds that my own elements change without complaint.

support.quote: Why then do you say that all things have come about badly and all things will always go badly
support.follows: It is wrong to say that everything has gone badly and always will.

support.quote: Loss is nothing other than change.

support.quote: The parts of the whole, all that are by nature contained by the universe, must perish; but let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered”.
support.follows: The parts of the universe must perish, and here perishing means being altered.

support.follows: My elements, which are also the universe’s, change and do not complain of it.
gives: The elements I am made of change too, and do not grumble

claims.t: Even if no nature orders things, a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of: it goes back where it came from, or its elements are scattered. Either way it is ridiculous to be surprised or annoyed at it.
claims.shared: 10.7 and 7.27 both give two accounts of dissolution, and both name “a scattering of the elements” among them (7.27: “some such scattering of elements”). 10.7 and 8.16 both say that a thing is dissolved into what it was made of (“into the things out of which each is put together”; “dissolved into what is its own”).
claims.changed: In 7.27 the second account is the atomists’; in 10.7 the person imagined leaves out nature as the one who orders things. The claim takes both as what still holds without nature. 10.7 speaks of parts of the whole; “a thing’s death” follows 8.16’s “what has died”.

support.quote: And if someone were to leave nature out of it and explain these things by the way they naturally are, even so it would be ridiculous to say that the parts of the whole are naturally such as to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though at something happening against nature, especially when the dissolution is into the things out of which each is put together.
support.follows: Even without nature as the one who orders things, it is absurd to expect change and then be annoyed when a thing comes apart into its parts.
gives: Even if no nature orders things
a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of
it is ridiculous to be surprised or annoyed at it

support.quote: For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the breath-like into the airy, so that these too are taken back up into the reason of the whole
support.follows: Dissolving either scatters a thing’s elements or turns them into earth and air, which the whole takes back.
gives: it goes back where it came from
its elements are scattered

support.quote: What grew from earth goes back to earth, and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air, back to the vault of heaven.
support.follows: What came from the earth returns to the earth, and what came from the sky returns to the sky.
gives: it goes back where it came from

support.quote: Or else this is a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms, and some such scattering of elements that cannot be affected.
support.follows: Or else death is a coming apart of the atoms’ links and a scattering of elements that nothing can act upon.
gives: a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of
its elements are scattered

support.quote: What has died does not fall outside the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into what is its own
support.follows: What dies stays in the universe, changes there, and is dissolved into its own parts.
gives: a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of

single.quote: But the sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toils without lament.
single.label: Without lament
single.t: What the gods send me I bear, in toil and without lament.
single.why: A line of verse Marcus copied, and the only place in the section that speaks of bearing what the gods send. 8.16 says the elements change without grumbling, but it speaks of the elements, not of what I bear.
single.follows: What the gods send must be borne, with toil and without lament.

single.quote: For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come from it. But you picture as seeds only those that are cast into earth or womb, and that is very much a layman’s view.
single.label: Everything a seed
single.t: Everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will come from it, and not only what is sown in the earth or in a womb.
single.why: Only this passage calls everything a seed. It goes with the claim that nature makes new things like the old, but no second passage says it.
single.follows: Whatever exists is a seed of what will follow it, not only seeds sown in earth or womb.

single.quote: Everything you see will very quickly perish, and those who have looked on as it perished will very quickly perish themselves, and whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with the one who died before their time.
single.label: Old and young alike
single.t: Everything I see will soon perish, and so will those who watched it perish; whoever dies very old will be brought level with whoever died before their time.
single.why: Only this passage draws from the speed of change that a long life and a short one end level. The speed itself is in claim 1.
single.follows: Since everything and everyone perishes quickly, dying very old comes to the same as dying young.

single.quote: except this: to act as your own nature leads, and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
single.label: What is great
single.t: The one thing I count as great is to act as my own nature leads and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
single.why: Only this passage names what is still great when nothing that passes is. It is kept beside the claim it limits.
single.follows: The only thing to picture as great is acting as one’s own nature leads and undergoing what the common nature brings.

members.text:
All parts of the world, (all things I mean that are contained
within the whole world), must of necessity at some time or other come to
corruption. Alteration I should say, to speak truly and properly; but
that I may be the better understood, I am content at this time to use
that more common word. Now say I, if so be that this be both hurtful
unto them, and yet unavoidable, would not, thinkest thou, the whole
itself be in a sweet case, all the parts of it being subject to
alteration, yea and by their making itself fitted for corruption, as
consisting of things different and contrary? And did nature then either
of herself thus project and purpose the affliction and misery of her
parts, and therefore of purpose so made them, not only that haply they
might, but of necessity that they should fall into evil; or did not she
know what she did, when she made them? For either of these two to say,
is equally absurd. But to let pass nature in general, and to reason of
things particular according to their own particular natures; how absurd
and ridiculous is it, first to say that all parts of the whole are, by
their proper natural constitution, subject to alteration; and then when
any such thing doth happen, as when one doth fall sick and dieth, to
take on and wonder as though some strange thing had happened? Though
this besides might move not so grievously to take on when any such thing
doth happen, that whatsoever is dissolved, it is dissolved into those
things, whereof it was compounded. For every dissolution is either
a mere dispersion, of the elements into those elements again whereof
everything did consist, or a change, of that which is more solid into
earth; and of that which is pure and subtile or spiritual, into air.
So that by this means nothing is lost, but all resumed again into those
rational generative seeds of the universe; and this universe, either
after a certain period of time to lie consumed by fire, or by continual
changes to be renewed, and so for ever to endure. Now that solid and
spiritual that we speak of, thou must not conceive it to be that very
same, which at first was, when thou wert born. For alas! all this that
now thou art in either kind, either for matter of substance, or of life,
hath but two or three days ago partly from meats eaten, and partly from
air breathed in, received all its influx, being the same then in no
other respect, than a running river, maintained by the perpetual influx
and new supply of waters, is the same. That therefore which thou hast
since received, not that which came from thy mother, is that which
comes to change and corruption. But suppose that that for the general
substance, and more solid part of it, should still cleave unto thee
never so close, yet what is that to the proper qualities and affections
of it, by which persons are distinguished, which certainly are quite
different?
members.english: The parts of the whole, all that are by nature contained by the universe, must perish; but let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered”. Now if this is by nature both bad and necessary for them, the whole would not be well managed, with its parts going into alteration and built in various ways for perishing. For did nature itself set out to treat its own parts badly, and to make them both liable to fall into what is bad and bound by necessity to fall into what is bad, or did such things come about without nature noticing? For both are unbelievable. And if someone were to leave nature out of it and explain these things by the way they naturally are, even so it would be ridiculous to say that the parts of the whole are naturally such as to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though at something happening against nature, especially when the dissolution is into the things out of which each is put together. For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the breath-like into the airy, so that these too are taken back up into the reason of the whole, whether the whole is burned up in fire at each cycle or renewed by everlasting exchanges. And do not picture the solid and the breath-like as the ones that date from the first birth. For all of this took its inflow yesterday and the day before, from food and from the air drawn in. So what changes is this that it took in, not what your mother bore. But suppose that this binds you very closely to that individually qualified thing, which, I think, has no bearing on what is being said now.
members.greek: Τοῖς μέρεσι τοῦ ὅλου, ὅσα φύσει περιέχεται ὑπὸ τοῦ κόσμου, ἀνάγκη φθείρεσθαι· λεγέσθω δὲ τοῦτο σημαντικῶς τοῦ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι. εἰ δὲ φύσει κακόν τε καὶ ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τοῦτο αὐτοῖς, οὐκ ἂν τὸ ὅλον καλῶς διεξάγοιτο τῶν μερῶν εἰς ἀλλοίωσιν ἰόντων καὶ πρὸς τὸ φθείρεσθαι διαφόρως κατεσκευασμένων. πότερον γὰρ ἐπεχείρησεν ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ τὰ ἑαυτῆς μέρη κακοῦν καὶ περιπτωτικὰ τῷ κακῷ καὶ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἔμπτωτα εἰς τὸ κακὸν ποιεῖν, ἢ ἔλαθεν αὐτὴν τοιάδε τινὰ γινόμενα; ἀμφότερα γὰρ ἀπίθανα. εἰ δέ τις καὶ ἀφέμενος τῆς φύσεως κατὰ τὸ πεφυκέναι ταῦτα ἐξηγοῖτο, καὶ ὣς γελοῖον ἅμα μὲν φάναι πεφυκέναι τὰ μέρη τοῦ ὅλου μεταβάλλειν, ἅμα δὲ ὡς ἐπί τινι τῶν παρὰ φύσιν συμβαίνοντι θαυμάζειν ἣ δυσχεραίνειν, ἄλλως τε καὶ τῆς διαλύσεως εἰς ταῦτα γινομένης, ἐξ ὧν ἕκαστον συνίσταται. ἤτοι γὰρ σκεδασμὸς στοιχείων, ἐξ ὧν συνεκρίθη, ἢ τροπὴ τοῦ μὲν στερεμνίου εἰς τὸ γεῶδες, τοῦ δὲ πνευματικοῦ εἰς τὸ ἀερῶδες, ὥστε καὶ ταῦτα ἀναληφθῆναι εἰς τὸν τοῦ ὅλου λόγον, εἴτε κατὰ περίοδον ἐκπυρουμένου εἴτε ἀιδίοις ἀμοιβαῖς ἀνανεουμένου. καὶ τὸ στερέμνιον δὲ καὶ τὸ πνευματικὸν μὴ φαντάζου τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης γενέσεως· πᾶν γὰρ τοῦτο ἐχθὲς καὶ τρίτην ἡμέραν ἐκ τῶν σιτίων καὶ τοῦ ἑλκομένου ἀέρος τὴν ἐπιρροὴν ἔλαβεν· τοῦτο οὖν ὃ ἔλαβε μεταβάλλει, οὐχ ὃ ἡ μήτηρ ἔτεκεν. ὑπόθου δ’ ὅτι ἐκείνῳ σε λίαν προσπλέκει τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ, οὐδὲν ὄντι οἶμαι πρὸς τὸ νῦν λεγόμενον.

members.text:
To look back upon things of former ages, as upon the manifold
changes and conversions of several monarchies and commonwealths. We
may also foresee things future, for they shall all be of the same kind;
neither is it possible that they should leave the tune, or break the
concert that is now begun, as it were, by these things that are now done
and brought to pass in the world. It comes all to one therefore, whether
a man be a spectator of the things of this life but forty years, or
whether he see them ten thousand years together: for what shall he
see more? 'And as for those parts that came from the earth, they shall
return unto the earth again; and those that came from heaven, they
also shall return unto those heavenly places.' Whether it be a mere
dissolution and unbinding of the manifold intricacies and entanglements
of the confused atoms; or some such dispersion of the simple and
incorruptible elements... 'With meats and drinks and divers charms, they
seek to divert the channel, that they might not die. Yet must we needs
endure that blast of wind that cometh from above, though we toil and
labour never so much.'
members.english:
Look back over what has gone before: so many changes of ruling powers. It is possible to foresee what will be as well. For it will certainly be of the same kind, and it cannot step out of the rhythm of what is happening now. So to observe human life for forty years is equal to observing it for ten thousand. For what more will you see?

And: “What grew from earth goes back to earth, and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air, back to the vault of heaven.” Or else this is a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms, and some such scattering of elements that cannot be affected.

And: “Turning the channel aside with food and drink and spells, so as not to die.” … “But the sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toils without lament.”

members.text:
Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even
whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished. Perpetual
fluxes and alterations renew the world, as the perpetual course of time
doth make the age of the world (of itself infinite) to appear always
fresh and new. In such a flux and course of all things, what of these
things that hasten so fast away should any man regard, since among all
there is not any that a man may fasten and fix upon? as if a man would
settle his affection upon some ordinary sparrow living by him, who is no
sooner seen, than out of sight. For we must not think otherwise of our
lives, than as a mere exhalation of blood, or of an ordinary respiration
of air. For what in our common apprehension is, to breathe in the air
and to breathe it out again, which we do daily: so much is it and no
more, at once to breathe out all thy respirative faculty into that
common air from whence but lately (as being but from yesterday, and
to-day), thou didst first breathe it in, and with it, life.
members.english: Some things are hurrying to come to be, others are hurrying to have come to be, and of what is coming to be some part has already been quenched. Flows and alterations renew the universe continually, just as the unbroken movement of time keeps boundless eternity always new. In this river, then, which of these things running past would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on? It is as if someone began to love one of the little sparrows flying past, and it has already gone out of sight. Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind: like the vapour that rises from blood and the breath drawn in from the air. For drawing in the air once and giving it back, which we do every moment, is the same kind of thing as giving back the whole power of breathing, which you acquired yesterday and the day before when you were born, to the place from which you first drew it.
members.greek: Τὰ μὲν σπεύδει γίνεσθαι, τὰ δὲ σπεύδει γεγονέναι, καὶ τοῦ γινομένου δὲ ἤδη τι ἀπέσβη· ῥύσεις καὶ ἀλλοιώσεις ἀνανεοῦσι τὸν κόσμον διηνεκῶς, ὥσπερ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἡ τοῦ χρόνου ἀδιάλειπτος φορὰ νέον ἀεὶ παρέχεται. ἐν δὴ τούτῳ τῷ ποταμῷ τί ἄν τις τούτων τῶν παραθεόντων ἐκτιμήσειεν, ἐφ’ οὗ στῆναι οὐκ ἔξεστιν; ὥσπερ εἴ τίς τι τῶν παραπετομένων στρουθαρίων φιλεῖν ἄρχοιτο, τὸ δ’ ἤδη ἐξ ὀφθαλμῶν ἀπελήλυθεν. τοιοῦτον δή τι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ ζωὴ ἑκάστου, οἷον ἡ ἀφ’ αἵματος ἀναθυμίασις καὶ ἡ ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἀνάπνευσις· ὁποῖον γάρ ἐστι τὸ ἅπαξ ἑλκύσαι τὸν ἀέρα καὶ ἀποδοῦναι, ὅπερ παρέκαστον ποιοῦμεν, τοιοῦτόν ἐστι καὶ τὸ τὴν πᾶσαν ἀναπνευστικὴν δύναμιν, ἣν χθὲς καὶ πρῴην ἀποτεχθεὶς ἐκτήσω, ἀποδοῦναι ἐκεῖ ὅθεν τὸ πρῶτον ἔσπασας.

members.text:
Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence;
all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves,
incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change
and alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that
the nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering
those things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we
may say, that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which
shall be. For if thou think that that only is seed, which either the
earth or the womb receiveth, thou art very simple.
members.english:
Everything lasts a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

Observe continually that all things come about by change, and accustom yourself to the thought that the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and make new things like them. For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come from it. But you picture as seeds only those that are cast into earth or womb, and that is very much a layman’s view.
members.greek:
Πᾶν ἐφήμερον, καὶ τὸ μνημονεῦον καὶ τὸ μνημονευόμενον.

Θεώρει διηνεκῶς πάντα κατὰ μεταβολὴν γινόμενα καὶ ἐθίζου ἐννοεῖν, ὅτι οὐδὲν οὕτως φιλεῖ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ὡς τὸ τὰ ὄντα μεταβάλλειν καὶ ποιεῖν νέα ὅμοια. σπέρμα γὰρ τρόπον τινὰ πᾶν τὸ ὃν τοῦ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐσομένου, σὺ δὲ μόνα σπέρματα φαντάζῃ τὰ εἰς γῆν ἣ μήτραν καταβαλλόμενα, τοῦτο δὲ λίαν ἰδιωτικόν.

members.text:
Ever to represent unto thyself; and to set before thee, both the
general age and time of the world, and the whole substance of it. And
how all things particular in respect of these are for their substance,
as one of the least seeds that is: and for their duration, as the
turning of the pestle in the mortar once about. Then to fix thy mind
upon every particular object of the world, and to conceive it, (as it
is indeed,) as already being in the state of dissolution, and of change;
tending to some kind of either putrefaction or dispersion; or whatsoever
else it is, that is the death as it were of everything in his own kind.
members.english:
An impression, constantly, of the whole of eternity and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, set against substance, a fig seed, and set against time, a turn of a drill.

Fixing attention on each object, think of it as already dissolving and in change, and as it were in the course of rotting or scattering, or in whatever way it is the nature of each thing, so to speak, to die.
members.greek:
Τοῦ ὅλου αἰῶνος καὶ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας συνεχῶς φαντασία καὶ ὅτι πάντα τὰ κατὰ μέρος, ὡς μὲν πρὸς οὐσίαν, κεγχραμίς, ὡς δὲ πρὸς χρόνον, τρυπάνου περιστροφή.

Εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἐφιστάντα ἐπινοεῖν αὐτὸ ἤδη διαλυόμενον καὶ ἐν μεταβολῇ καὶ οἷον σήψει ἢ σκεδάσει γινόμενον ἢ καθότι ἕκαστον πέφυκεν ὥσπερ θνῄσκειν.

members.text:
To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole
course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy
thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object. How short
the time is from the generation of anything, unto the dissolution of
the same; but how immense and infinite both that which was before the
generation, and that which after the generation of it shall be. All
things that thou seest, will soon be perished, and they that see their
corruptions, will soon vanish away themselves. He that dieth a hundred
years old, and he that dieth young, shall come all to one.
members.english:
By having encompassed the whole universe in thought, and by surveying everlasting eternity, and by thinking of the swift change of each particular thing: how short is the stretch from coming to be to dissolution, and how gaping the time before the coming to be, just as the time after the dissolution is likewise boundless.

Everything you see will very quickly perish, and those who have looked on as it perished will very quickly perish themselves, and whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with the one who died before their time.
members.greek:
τῷ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον περιειληφέναι τῇ γνώμῃ καὶ τὸν ἀίδιον αἰῶνα περινοεῖν καὶ τὴν τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἑκάστου πράγματος ταχεῖαν μεταβολὴν ἐπινοεῖν, ὡς βραχὺ μὲν τὸ ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι διαλύσεως, ἀχανὲς δὲ τὸ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως, ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον.

Πάντα ὅσα ὁρᾷς τάχιστα φθαρήσεται καὶ οἱ φθειρόμενα αὐτὰ ἐπιδόντες τάχιστα καὶ αὐτοὶ φθαρήσονται καὶ ὁ ἐσχατόγηρως ἀποθανὼν εἰς ἴσον καταστήσεται τῷ προώρῳ.

members.text:
Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself
shall have her change. And then the course will be, from one period of
eternity unto another, and so a perpetual eternity. Now can any man
that shall consider with himself in his mind the several rollings or
successions of so many changes and alterations, and the swiftness of all
these rulings; can he otherwise but contemn in his heart and despise
all worldly things? The cause of the universe is as it were a strong
torrent, it carrieth all away.
members.english:
Any moment now earth will cover us all. Then earth itself will change, and those things too will change without end, and those again without end. For a person who reflects on wave after wave of changes and alterations, and on their speed, will look down on everything mortal.

The substance of the whole is a torrent: it carries everything along.
members.greek:
Ἤδη πάντας ἡμᾶς γῆ καλύψει, ἔπειτα καὶ αὐτὴ μεταβαλεῖ κἀκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον μεταβαλεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἐκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον. τὰς γὰρ ἐπικυματώσεις τῶν μεταβολῶν καὶ ἀλλοιώσεων ἐνθυμούμενός τις καὶ τὸ τάχος παντὸς θνητοῦ καταφρονήσει.

Χειμάρρους ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία· πάντα φέρει.

members.text:
All things that are in the world, are always in the estate
of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under
corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
members.english: All things are in change. You yourself too are in continual alteration and, in a certain respect, in perishing, and so is the whole universe.
members.greek: Πάντα ἐν μεταβολῇ· καὶ αὐτὸς σὺ ἐν διηνεκεῖ ἀλλοιώσει καὶ κατά τι φθορᾷ, καὶ ὁ κόσμος δὲ ὅλος.

members.text:
Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the
bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the
world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world.
Consider the nature of all worldly sensible things; of those especially,
which either ensnare by pleasure, or for their irksomeness are dreadful,
or for their outward lustre and show are in great esteem and request,
how vile and contemptible, how base and corruptible, how destitute of
all true life and being they are.
members.english: How quickly all things vanish, the bodies themselves into the universe, the memories of them into eternity. What all the things perceived by the senses are like, and above all those that lure with pleasure or frighten with pain or are loudly celebrated through vanity: how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead.
members.greek: Πῶς πάντα ταχέως ἐναφανίζεται, τῷ μὲν κόσμῳ αὐτὰ τὰ σώματα, τῷ δὲ αἰῶνι αἱ μνῆμαι αὐτῶν. οἶά ἐστι τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα καὶ μάλιστα τὰ ἡδονῇ δελεάζοντα ἢ τῷ πόνῳ φοβοῦντα ἢ τῷ τύφῳ διαβεβοημένα· πῶς εὐτελῆ καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητα καὶ ῥυπαρὰ καὶ εὔφθαρτα καὶ νεκρά,

members.text:
What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is
allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general
age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also
what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of
the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl. After thou
shalt rightly have considered these things with thyself; fancy not
anything else in the world any more to be of any weight and moment
but this, to do that only which thine own nature doth require; and to
conform thyself to that which the common nature doth afford.
members.english: How small a part of boundless, gaping eternity has been portioned out to each one: for it vanishes very quickly into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the whole of soul. And on how small a clod of the whole earth you crawl. Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great except this: to act as your own nature leads, and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
members.greek: Πόστον μέρος τοῦ ἀπείρου καὶ ἀχανοῦς αἰῶνος ἀπομεμέρισται ἑκάστῳ· τάχιστα γὰρ ἐναφανίζεται τῷ ἀιδίῳ· πόστον δὲ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας· πόστον δὲ τῆς ὅλης ψυχῆς· ἐν πόστῳ δὲ βωλαρίῳ τῆς ὅλης γῆς ἕρπεις. πάντα ταῦτα ἐνθυμούμενος μηδὲν μέγα φαντάζου ἢ τό, ὡς μὲν ἡ σὴ φύσις ἄγει ποιεῖν, πάσχειν δὲ ὡς ἡ κοινὴ φύσις φέρει.

members.text:
He that seeth the things that are now, hath Seen all that either
was ever, or ever shall be, for all things are of one kind; and all like
one unto another. Meditate often upon the connection of all things in
the world; and upon the mutual relation that they have one unto another.
For all things are after a sort folded and involved one within another,
and by these means all agree well together. For one thing is consequent
unto another, by local motion, by natural conspiration and agreement,
and by substantial union, or, reduction of all substances into one.
members.english:
Whoever has seen what is now has seen everything: all that has come to be from the everlasting past and all that will be without end. For all things are of the same stock and of the same kind.

Reflect often on the linking together of all things in the universe and their relation to one another. For in a way all things are interwoven with one another, and all are on that account dear to one another. For this thing is next in order to another, through the movement of tension, the breathing together and the unity of substance.
members.greek:

Πολλάκις ἐνθυμοῦ τὴν ἐπισύνδεσιν πάντων τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ σχέσιν πρὸς ἄλληλα. τρόπον γάρ τινα πάντα ἀλλήλοις ἐπιπέπλεκται καὶ πάντα κατὰ τοῦτο φίλα ἀλλήλοις ἐστί· καὶ γὰρ ἄλλῳ ἑξῆς ἐστι τοῦτο διὰ τὴν τονικὴν κίνησιν καὶ σύμπνοιαν καὶ τὴν ἕνωσιν τῆς οὐσίας.

members.text:
To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to
attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and
swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in
the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away,
another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
members.english:
There is nothing bad for things that are in the course of change, just as there is nothing good for things that come to exist out of change.

Eternity is a kind of river of things that come to be, and a violent current. For as soon as each thing has been seen it has been carried past, and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along.
members.greek:
Οὐδέν ἐστι κακὸν τοῖς ἐν μεταβολῇ γινομένοις, ὡς οὐδὲ ἀγαθὸν τοῖς ἐκ μεταβολῆς ὑφισταμένοις.

Ποταμός τίς ἐστι τῶν γινομένων καὶ ῥεῦμα βίαιον ὁ αἰών· ἅμα τε γὰρ ὤφθη ἕκαστον, καὶ παρενήνεκται καὶ ἄλλο παραφέρεται, τὸ δὲ ἐνεχθήσεται.

members.english: The nature of the whole has this as its work: to move what is here over to there, to change it, to lift it from here and carry it there. All things are transformations, not so that one need fear something new. All things are familiar, and what is more, the allotments are equal.
members.greek: Ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις τοῦτο ἔργον ἔχει, τὰ ὧδε ὄντα ἐκεῖ μετατιθέναι, μεταβάλλειν, αἴρειν ἔνθεν καὶ ἐκεῖ φέρειν. πάντα τροπαί, οὐχ ὥστε φοβηθῆναι, μή τι καινόν· πάντα συνήθη· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἴσαι αἱ ἀπονεμήσεις.

members.text:
Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and
alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most
delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is
well done. For that was the estate of worldly things from the beginning,
and so shall it ever be. Or wouldest thou rather say, that all things
in the world have gone ill from the beginning for so many ages, and
shall ever go ill? And then among so many deities, could no divine power
be found all this while, that could rectify the things of the world? Or
is the world, to incessant woes and miseries, for ever condemned?
members.english: Loss is nothing other than change. And in this the nature of the whole delights, the nature in accordance with which all things come about well, and from eternity have come about in the same kind of way, and without end there will be others like them. Why then do you say that all things have come about badly and all things will always go badly, and that among so many gods no power, it seems, has ever been found to set these things right, but the universe has been condemned to be held fast in bad things without a break?
members.greek: Ἡ ἀποβολὴ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ μεταβολή. τούτῳ δὲ χαίρει ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, καθ’ ἢν πάντα καλῶς γίνεται καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ὁμοειδῶς ἐγίνετο καὶ εἰς ἄπειρον τοιαῦθ̓ ἕτερα ἔσται. τί οὖν λέγεις ὅτι ἐγίνετό τε πάντα κακῶς καὶ πάντα ἀεὶ κακῶς ἔσται καὶ οὐδεμία ἄρα δύναμις ἐν τοσούτοις θεοῖς ἐξευρέθη ποτὲ ἡ διορθώσουσα ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ κατακέκριται ὁ κόσμος ἐν ἀδιαλείπτοις κακοῖς συνέχεσθαι;

members.text:
Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die
and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode
and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper
elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which
thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why
shouldest thou?
members.english: What has died does not fall outside the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into what is its own, which are the elements of the universe and of you. And these too change, and do not grumble.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 7.27 is 7.49–51, 6.14 is 6.15, 4.29 is 4.35–36, 10.19 is 10.17–18, 9.31 is 9.32b–33, 9.27 is 9.28b–29a, 9.17 is 9.19, 2.9 is 2.12a, 12.25 is 12.32, 6.34 is 6.37–38, 4.35 is 4.42–43, 8.5 is 8.6, 9.33 is 9.35 and 8.16 is 8.18; 10.7 is the same.
Reads “perish” in 10.7, “perishing” in 9.17 and “loss” in 9.33 as one thing, because 10.7 and 9.33 each say that it is change.

Sets “nothing that passes is great” beside “nothing bad” in the statement. 4.35 pairs a denial of bad with a denial of good in one sentence, but the statement’s “great” comes from 12.25, 9.27, 6.14 and 2.9, not from 4.35.

Leaves out what belongs to other articles: that what I give back at death I took in only “yesterday and the day before” (10.7, 6.14), the subject of Article 33; that all things are linked and dear to one another (6.34), Article 4’s subject; and the changes of ruling powers that open 7.27.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that I accept what happens without complaint, which claim 5 comes near, and that none of it is unusual, which claim 2’s “nothing comes that is new in kind” comes near, though claim 2 speaks of one kind across all time, not of the ordinariness of what happens to me; Article 5 says that nature makes new things of what it takes back. Claims 5 and 6 come near Article 36 (no change of my life, its ending included, is bad) and Article 10 (death is a dissolving of my elements), the said-once 9.31 is Article 35’s point that a long life and a short one come to the same, and claims 2 and 6 come near Articles 30 and 33 on sameness and on matter reshaped. What this article adds is change itself, in all things and not only in my death: it is everywhere, fast and of one kind, it is nothing bad, and nothing that passes is great.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claims 1, 2 and 3 each gain a second author, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: an exercise for facing death, what failing looks like and the way back, and what holds if death is simply the end. He limits claim 4: death is no evil, but it keeps a look of evil.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and takes in the other case: if death is simply an end and not a crossing, ceasing is the same as never having begun.

items.role: If death is simply the end
items.t: Death is either an end or a crossing. If it is an end, I do not fear ceasing: it is the same as never having begun, and a lamp is no worse off when it is put out than before it was lit.
items.why: Marcus’s passages here hold that nothing of me goes into nothing; none asks what is left if death is simply the end. Seneca takes that case and answers it: ceasing is the same as not having begun.

passages.title: On an old man's calm before death
passages.text: Death has a necessity that is fair and cannot be overcome: who can complain of being in a condition that no one is not in? And the first part of fairness is equality. But at this point it is needless to plead the case of nature, who wanted our law to be no other than her own: whatever she has put together she takes apart, and whatever she has taken apart she puts together again.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: All things move through fixed periods: they must be born, grow, be extinguished. Whatever you see running above us, and these things on which we lean and have been set as though they were the most solid of things, will be worn away and will cease. There is nothing that does not have its own old age. Nature sends these things off to the same place after unequal spans: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.

passages.title: On the benefits of a quiet life
passages.text: But if so great a desire for a longer life has hold of you, consider that none of the things that go out of sight and are put back into the nature of things, from which they came out and will soon come forth, is used up: these things stop, they do not perish, and death, which we dread and refuse, interrupts life, it does not snatch it away; a day will come again to put us back into the light, a day that many would refuse if it did not bring them back with their memory gone.

passages.title: On causes and the worth of studying nature
passages.text: The place that god holds in this world, the mind holds in a human being; what matter is there, the body is in us. So let the worse serve the better. Let us be brave against the things of chance; let us not tremble at wrongs, at wounds, at chains, at want. What is death? Either an end or a crossing. I am not afraid of ceasing, for it is the same as not having begun; nor of crossing over, because nowhere shall I be so cramped. Farewell.

passages.title: On asthma and rehearsing death
passages.text: I ask you, would you not call it most foolish if someone thought that a lamp is worse off when it has been put out than before it is lit? We too are both put out and lit: in the time between we go through something, but on either side there is deep freedom from care. For this, my Lucilius, unless I am mistaken, is where we go wrong: we judge that death follows, when it has both gone before and will follow. Whatever was before us is death; for what does it matter whether you do not begin or you cease, when the result of both is this, not to be?

passages.title: On facing death without logical tricks
passages.text: So even if death is a matter of indifference, it is still not a thing that can easily be disregarded: the mind must be hardened by much training to bear the sight of it and its approach. Death ought to be scorned more than it usually is; for we have believed many things about it; the talents of many have competed to increase its bad name; a prison in the underworld has been described, and a region weighed down by everlasting night, in which the huge doorkeeper of Orcus, lying on half-eaten bones in his bloody cave, barking for ever, frightens the bloodless shades. Even when you have persuaded people that these are stories and that nothing is left for the dead to fear, another fear comes up: for they are equally afraid of being in the underworld and of being nowhere.

passages.title: On withdrawing from a busy career
passages.text: “No one,” he says, “goes out of life otherwise than as he was born.” That is false: we die worse than we are born. That fault is ours, not nature’s. She ought to remonstrate with us and say: “What is this? I gave birth to you without desires, without fears, without superstition, without treachery and the other plagues: go out such as you came in.”

passages.title: On facing death without logical tricks
passages.text: Among these things too, Lucilius, which we call middle, there is a great difference. For death is not a matter of indifference in the same way as whether you have an even number of hairs: death is among those things that are not indeed evils, yet have the look of an evil. There is love of self, and an inborn will to last and to preserve oneself, and a shrinking from dissolution, [gap in the Latin text] because it seems to snatch many goods away from us and to lead us out of this plenty of things to which we have grown used. This too estranges us from death, that we already know the things here, while we do not know what the things are like to which we are going to cross over, and we shudder at the unknown. Besides, there is a natural fear of the dark, into which, it is believed, death will lead us.

single.quote: either they will go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or they will be scattered
single.label: One whole or not
single.t: Whether the stuff of the world is one continuous whole or not, what exists changes either way: if it is one, things go up in vapour; if it is not, they are scattered.
single.why: Only this passage gives two pictures of what the world is made of and says what happens to things under each. 5.13 also allows for another picture, but a different one, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: If the stuff of the world is one continuous whole, things will go up in vapour; if not, they will be scattered.

single.quote: and, for one who goes back, into another infinity. For nothing prevents one from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.
single.label: Even in finite cycles
single.t: Even if the universe is governed in cycles that come to an end, nothing stops me from saying that the change which made me and will pass me on is endless both ways: back through my parents and forward through my parts.
single.why: Only this passage asks whether the endless change still holds if the universe runs in cycles with an end. “So” covers both infinities 5.13 has just named, forward through my parts and back through my parents. 6.4 allows for a different picture, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Going back through one’s ancestors leads into another infinity, and one may say so even if the universe runs in finite cycles.

members.text:
The nature of the universe, of the common substance of all things
as it were of so much wax hath now perchance formed a horse; and then,
destroying that figure, hath new tempered and fashioned the matter of it
into the form and substance of a tree: then that again into the form and
substance of a man: and then that again into some other. Now every one
of these doth subsist but for a very little while. As for dissolution,
if it be no grievous thing to the chest or trunk, to be joined together;
why should it be more grievous to be put asunder?
members.english: The nature of the whole, out of the whole of substance as if out of wax, at one moment shaped a little horse; then it melted that down and used its material for a little tree, then for a little human, then for something else. Each of these existed for the briefest time. But there is nothing terrible for a little box in being taken apart, just as there is nothing good in its being put together.
members.greek: Ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ νῦν μὲν ἱππάριον ἔπλασε, συγχέασα δὲ τοῦτο εἰς δενδρύφιον συνεχρήσατο τῇ ὕλῃ αὐτοῦ· εἶτα εἰς ἀνθρωπάριον· εἶτα εἰς ἄλλο τι· ἕκαστον δὲ τούτων πρὸς ὀλίγιστον ὑπέστη. δεινὸν δὲ οὐδὲν τὸ διαλυθῆναι τῷ κιβωτίῳ, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ συμπαγῆναι ἀγαθόν.

members.text:
All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall
be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be
reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be
scattered and dispersed. As for that Rational Essence by which all
things are governed, as it best understandeth itself, both its own
disposition, and what it doth, and what matter it hath to do with and
accordingly doth all things; so we that do not, no wonder, if we wonder
at many things, the reasons whereof we cannot comprehend.
members.english:
All existing things will very quickly change, and either they will go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or they will be scattered.

The reason that governs knows in what condition it acts, what it does, and on what material.
members.greek:
Πάντα τὰ ὑποκείμενα τάχιστα μεταβαλεῖ καὶ ἤτοι ἐκθυμιαθήσεται, εἴπερ ἥνωται ἡ οὐσία, ἢ σκεδασθήσεται.

Ὁ διοικῶν λόγος οἶδε πῶς διακείμενος καὶ τί ποιεῖ καὶ ἐπὶ τίνος ὕλης.

members.text:
All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption
can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing
become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation
be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time
into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I
also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before
them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak,
though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods
of time limited, and confined.
members.english: I am made up of what is causal and what is material, and neither of these will perish into what is not, just as neither came to be out of what is not. So every part of me will be assigned, through change, to some part of the universe, and that in turn will change into another part of the universe, and so on to infinity. It was through a change of this kind that I too came to be, and my parents, and, for one who goes back, into another infinity. For nothing prevents one from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.
members.greek: Ἐξ αἰτιώδους καὶ ὑλικοῦ συνέστηκα, οὐδέτερον δὲ τούτων εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθαρήσεται, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος ὑπέστη. οὐκοῦν καταταχθήσεται πᾶν μέρος ἐμὸν κατὰ μεταβολὴν εἰς μέρος τι τοῦ κόσμου καὶ πάλιν ἐκεῖνο εἰς ἕτερον μέρος τι τοῦ κόσμου μεταβαλεῖ καὶ ἤδη εἰς ἄπειρον. κατὰ τοιαύτην δὲ μεταβολὴν κἀγὼ ὑπέστην καὶ οἱ ἐμὲ γεννήσαντες καὶ ἐπανιόντι εἰς ἄλλο ἄπειρον. οὐδὲν γὰρ κωλύει οὕτως φάναι, κἂν κατὰ περιόδους πεπερασμένας ὁ κόσμος διοικῆται.

members.text:
Whatsoever is material, doth soon vanish away into the common
substance of the whole; and whatsoever is formal, or, whatsoever doth
animate that which is material, is soon resumed into the common reason
of the whole; and the fame and memory of anything, is soon swallowed up
by the general age and duration of the whole.
members.english: Everything material very quickly vanishes into the substance of the whole, and every cause is very quickly taken back up into the reason of the whole, and the memory of everything is very quickly buried in eternity.
members.greek: Πᾶν τὸ ἔνυλον ἐναφανίζεται τάχιστα τῇ τῶν ὅλων οὐσίᾳ καὶ πᾶν αἴτιον εἰς τὸν τῶν ὅλων λόγον τάχιστα ἀναλαμβάνεται καὶ παντὸς μνήμη τάχιστα ἐγκαταχώννυται τῷ αἰῶνι.

members.text:
As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now
shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot
thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational
substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated.
Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops
first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
members.english:
You came to exist as a part within something. You will vanish into what gave birth to you; or rather, you will be taken back up into its seminal reason, through change.

Many little lumps of incense on the same altar: one fell earlier, another later, but it makes no difference.
members.greek:
Ἐνυπέστης ὡς μέρος. ἐναφανισθήσῃ τῷ γεννήσαντι· μᾶλλον δὲ ἀναληφθήσῃ εἰς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ τὸν σπερματικὸν κατὰ μεταβολήν.

Πολλὰ λιβανωτοῦ βωλάρια ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ βωμοῦ· τὸ μὲν προκατέπεσεν, τὸ δʼ ὕστερον, διαφέρει δʼ οὐδέν.

members.text:
As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a
mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing
surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal
events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto,
not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper
constitution of man himself.
members.english: Death is the same kind of thing as birth, a mystery of nature: a combining out of the same elements, a dissolving into the same. And in short, it is not a thing anyone would be ashamed of: for it is not contrary to what follows in sequence for a living being with mind, nor contrary to the reason on which it is built.
members.greek: Ὁ θάνατος τοιοῦτον, οἷον γένεσις, φύσεως μυστήριον· σύγκρισις ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν στοιχείων, εἰς ταὐτὰ λύσις. ὅλως δὲ οὐκ ἐφʼ ᾧ ἄν τις αἰσχυνθείη· οὐ γὰρ παρὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῷ νοερῷ ζῴῳ οὐδὲ παρὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς κατασκευῆς.

members.text:
I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I
fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which
continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of
whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her
blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have
been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that
tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or
so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.
members.english: I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest, breathing my last into that from which I draw breath every day, and falling on that from which my father gathered the bit of seed, my mother the bit of blood and my nurse the bit of milk; from which every day, for so many years, I have been fed and watered; which bears me as I tread on it and make free use of it for so many purposes.
members.greek: Πορεύομαι διὰ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν, μέχρι πεσὼν ἀναπαύσομαι ἐναποπνεύσας μὲν τούτῳ, ἐξ οὖ καθ’ ἡμέραν ἀναπνέω, πεσὼν δὲ ἐπὶ τούτῳ, ἐξ οὗ καὶ τὸ σπερμάτιον ὁ πατήρ μου συνέλεξε καὶ τὸ αἱμάτιον ἡ μήτηρ καὶ τὸ γαλάκτιον ἡ τροφός· ἐξ οὗ καθ’ ἡμέραν τοσούτοις ἔτεσι βόσκομαι καὶ ἀρδεύομαι· ὃ φέρει με πατοῦντα καὶ εἰς τοσαῦτα ἀποχρώμενον αὐτῷ.

members.text:
Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of
anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.
members.english: Nature has aimed at the ending of each thing not a bit less than at its beginning and its course.
members.greek: Ἡ φύσις ἐστόχασται ἑκάστου οὐδέν τι ἔλασσον τῆς ἀπολήξεως ἢ τῆς ἀρχῆς τε καὶ διεξαγωγῆς,

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 7.17 is 7.23, 6.4 is 6.4–5, 7.7 is 7.10, 4.12 is 4.14–15 and 8.18 is 8.20; 5.13, 4.5 and 5.4 are the same.

Reads the pair “what is causal and what is material” in 5.13 and the pair “every cause” and “everything material” in 7.7 as the same two things in me, and explains the cause as what in me acts and shapes the matter. In the statement, “the whole” that I came out of is the editor’s word for 4.5’s “the same elements”, 5.13’s parts of the universe and 4.12’s “something” of which I am a part.

Reads “a change of this kind” in 5.13 as the change just described, by which my parts pass into other parts of the universe. So 5.13 is taken to say that I came to be by the same kind of change as the one that ends me, and it backs “My death is the same kind of change as my birth” beside 4.5.

Applies 7.17’s last sentence, said of “a little box”, to me, since the human made of wax is one of the shapes in the same passage. Leaves out, as being about other things: the second saying of 6.4 (modern 6.5: the reason that governs knows on what material it acts) and of 4.12 (modern 4.15: lumps of incense falling earlier or later); 7.7’s “the memory of everything is very quickly buried in eternity”, which is about memory, not matter; 4.5’s “not a thing anyone would be ashamed of”, whose shame the passage does not explain (claim 4 quotes the reason that follows it); and 5.4’s “which bears me as I tread on it”, about how the earth serves me while I live.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this. Article 32 (“All things pass”) says that change is nothing bad for what is changed (its claim 5) and that a thing’s death is its dissolution into what it was made of (its claim 6). Article 10’s claim 4 says that death is a dissolving of my elements, according to nature, and so not bad. Article 36 says that my death is one more of the changes I live through (its claim 2) and that nature, not I, fixes the time and limit of my death, which is not bad (its claim 3). Claims 3 and 4 here come near all of these, and Ep. 30.11, 82.15 and 82.16 are used in Article 10 or 36 as well. Article 6 says once that everything is from nature and goes into nature (4.19), and Article 5 (its claim 3) that nature throws nothing away but takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it, which comes near claims 1 and 2 here; Ep. 36.10 is used there as well. What this article adds is that nothing of me perishes into nothing, that what I am made of is shaped into something else, that my death is the same change as my birth, and that my ending was intended as my beginning was. No passage gives an exercise or describes failing.
